segments.text: When you type a prompt into chat GPT, the AI instantly turns your words into individual tokens and maps them to mathematical vectors.
But mapping a word to a number isn't enough for true comprehension, because human language relies entirely on surrounding context.
Sometimes a word means different things depending on its neighbors.
Look at the word light in the left panel.
In the first sentence, light refers to brightness.
In the second, it means not heavy.
The AI has to decide which meaning to use based on words like turn on or carry.
Then there are pronouns.
In the right panel, look at the word it.
The cat drank the milk because it was thirsty.
The cat drank the milk because it was fresh.
By changing only the last word, we change whether it points to the cat or the milk.
While humans resolve these connections instantly, early computer models lacked a mechanical way to bridge the gap between words.
To understand why older AI struggled with these sentences, we have to look at how they were designed to read.
These systems operated sequentially.
They moved through text like a typewriter, processing one single word at a time in a rigid line.
You can see the flaw in this flowchart.
As the AI moves forward, earlier words slip from memory.
Here, there is a 10-word gap between cat and it.
This sequential pattern acts as a functional ceiling.
It is difficult for a machine to form complex connections if the earliest parts of a thought have already slipped away.
The architecture changed in 2017 when researchers at Google published a paper titled, Attention is All You Need.
This specific breakthrough is the engine inside every large language model we use today.
It is the T in chat GPT.
This diagram on the right shows the core difference.
The transformer model abandons sequential reading.
It ingests every word of a message at the exact same time.
Because the entire message arrives in a single parallel cluster, no data is left behind.
This removes the problem of words fading as the AI moves down the line.
Reading everything at once is just the first step.
The model then uses a two-part mechanical process to build an actual understanding of the text.
Step one is attention.
When the model encounters it, it scans every word heavily weighting its relationship with cat.
Step two is transformation.
The system updates the raw data for it using those weights, modifying it until it effectively means cat.
This creates a context-specific definition for each prompt.
The model's core dictionary remains unchanged.
Instead, it calculates these meanings fresh every time you hit enter.
The model builds these relationships on the fly.
It constructs meaning by analyzing the entire sentence as a single unit.
We can see the results of this process by looking back at the sentences from the beginning of the video.
Look at the panel on the left.
Attention links light to turn on or carry, shifting its meaning from brightness to weight.
On the right, it links it to thirsty or fresh, resolving the ambiguity.
The system repeats this for every part of your input.
Reading an entire prompt simultaneously creates a massive advantage, but it introduces a new logical paradox.
If an AI reads every word at the exact same time, it inherently destroys the chronology of the sentence.
Take a simple three-word phrase.
Dog bites man.
If the computer receives those three tokens all at once without knowing the sequence, they could easily be arranged as man bites dog.
The raw tokens are identical, but without sequence, the meaning is destroyed.
To solve this, the architecture includes an extra step before the first processing layer even begins.
A sequence number is mixed directly into the data pattern of every single token.
It stamps the vector with a signal saying, I am token number one, or I am token number two.
The technical name for this critical structural patch is positional encoding.
With positional encoding hard-coded into the tokens themselves, the entire paragraph can arrive simultaneously.
The AI gets the full computational benefit of simultaneous processing while preserving the linear narrative of human speech.
It is a massive computational task, but the core idea is simple.
Resolving the nuances of language comes down to accurately weighing the words that surround them.
Attention is all you need.
